content: GroEL is a member of the chaperonin family of molecular chaperones and is widely present in many bacterial species. It plays a critical role in ensuring the proper folding of numerous proteins. For its function, GroEL requires the assistance of a co-chaperonin protein complex called GroES, which acts as a lid-like structure. In eukaryotic cells, the proteins Hsp60 and Hsp10 are structurally and functionally analogous to GroEL and GroES, respectively. Within the cellular environment, the GroEL/GroES-mediated protein folding process involves multiple cycles of substrate protein binding, encapsulation, and release. Unfolded substrate proteins initially bind to hydrophobic regions located on the inner rim of the open cavity of GroEL, forming a binary complex with the chaperonin. This binding, along with ATP binding, triggers a conformational change in GroEL that facilitates the attachment of the binary complex to the GroES lid structure. When GroES binds to the open cavity of GroEL, it induces a rotational movement in the individual subunits of GroEL. This rotation eliminates the hydrophobic substrate-binding sites from the cavity's interior, causing the substrate protein to be released into the now predominantly hydrophilic chamber. The hydrophilic environment within the chamber promotes the burial of hydrophobic residues in the substrate protein, thereby driving its folding. ATP hydrolysis and the binding of a new substrate protein to the opposite cavity of GroEL generate an allosteric signal. This signal leads to the release of GroES and the encapsulated protein into the cytosol. A given substrate protein may undergo several rounds of folding, returning to its unfolded state each time, until it achieves its native conformation or an intermediate structure committed to reaching the native state. Alternatively, the substrate protein may undergo competing reactions, such as misfolding or aggregation with other misfolded proteins. The thermodynamics of the GroEL complex strongly favor compact molecular conformations of the substrate protein. In free solution, long-range non-polar interactions are entropically costly. However, within the confined space of the GroEL complex, the relative entropy loss is significantly reduced. The capture mechanism of GroEL tends to segregate non-polar binding sites from polar ones. When the non-polar surfaces of GroEL are removed, the likelihood of a non-polar group encountering an intramolecular non-polar site is much higher than in bulk solution. The hydrophobic sites, initially exposed on the exterior, are gathered together at the top of the cis domain and bind to one another. The geometry of GroEL ensures that polar structures lead the folding process, enveloping the non-polar core as it emerges from the trans side. Structurally, GroEL is a dual-ringed tetradecamer, with each ring (cis and trans) composed of seven subunits. Conformational changes within the central cavity of GroEL transform its interior from hydrophobic to hydrophilic, a property that likely facilitates protein folding. The activity of GroEL is rooted in the structure of its monomer. The Hsp60 monomer consists of three distinct sections separated by two hinge regions. The apical section contains numerous hydrophobic binding sites for unfolded protein substrates. Globular proteins typically do not bind to the apical domain because their hydrophobic regions are buried internally, away from the aqueous medium, which is thermodynamically optimal. Consequently, these substrate sites only bind to proteins that are not optimally folded. The apical domain also contains binding sites for the Hsp10 monomers of GroES. The equatorial domain features a slot near the hinge point for ATP binding, as well as two attachment points for the other half of the GroEL molecule. The remainder of the equatorial section is moderately hydrophilic. The addition of ATP and GroES induces significant conformational changes in the cis domain of GroEL. These changes are mediated by flexion and rotation at the two hinge points of the Hsp60 monomers. The intermediate domain folds downward and inward by approximately 25° at the lower hinge. This cooperative flexing of all monomers increases the equatorial diameter of the GroEL cage. Simultaneously, the apical domain rotates upward and outward by 60° at the upper hinge and rotates 90° around the hinge axis. This motion opens the top of the cis domain widely, while completely removing the substrate-binding sites from the interior of the cage. GroEL has been shown to interact with GroES, ALDH2, Caspase 3, and Dihydrofolate reductase.
